newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rebels capture key airport in east Zaire - U.N.
newsitem.headline: Rebels capture key airport in east Zaire - U.N.

text.p: Tutsi fighters on Thursday seized the airport in the eastern Zairean city of Goma, centre for refugee relief operations in the region, a U.N. official said.
Panos Moumtzis, spokesman in Goma for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), told Reuters: "The airport has been taken over. It is confirmed from the Zairean side."
"Right now there is no movement in town. It is completely deserted," said Moumtzis, adding aid workers remained inside their offices in the lakeside city after heavy fighting since Thursday morning.
Goma is the main centre for international aid efforts to feed about 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees inside Zaire. The airport is about five km (three miles) north of the city.

The fast-moving conflict in eastern Zaire began with a Zairean army campaign against Tutsis but springs from deadly rivalry between Tutsis and Hutus which killed up to one million people in Rwanda's 1994 genocide and left Zaire hosting the Hutu refugees.
Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko has been living at a luxury hotel in Lausanne, Switzerland for more than two months, undergoing cancer treatment as the east of his country slides into anarchy.
Aid workers are desperately concerned about the plight of the Rwandan refugees. "We are very worried about how we can continue humanitarian assistance," said Moumtzis.
"It feels like a war. As of this morning we feel the fighting is very close and the circle is getting tighter," said Moumtzis earlier, before reporting the capture of the airport.
Aid workers in Goma, the North Kivu provincial capital, were awoken by firing on the edge of the city in the early morning.

Incoming and outgoing mortar bombs and heavy weapons fire centred on an area about two km (one mile) north of the city limits and from the Rwandan border I saw mortar bombs explode in the outskirts of Goma.

"There is a general feeling of law and order breaking down with two UNHCR vehicles hijacked this morning. Some aid agency compounds and offices have been attacked by Zairean soldiers and looting is under way but it is still limited," Moumtzis told Reuters.
He said leaders in Kahindo camp north of Goma with some 110,000 residents decided on Wednesday to move towards Mugunga camp, to the west of the city, and had done so at first light.
"They are now taking a path through the mountains," he said.
"Machinegun and rifle fire turned in the last three hours into mortars," said Michelle Quintaglie, spokeswoman for the World Food Programme in Goma. "The situation has deteriorated very rapidly."
She said the first Zairean and Rwandan refugees of the day were starting to arrive in Mugunga, already the world's largest refugee camp crammed with an estimated 400,000 residents.
The Roman Catholic archbishop of the town of Bukavu, south of Goma, was killed on Tuesday and two Spanish priests were separately held hostage in the town under attack from Tutsi rebels.
It was not clear who controlled Bukavu, a lakeside city across from the Rwandan border. Some residents in radio accounts spoke of looting and the presence of Rwandan commandos.

As violence escalated, the special envoy appointed by the United Nations to bring an end to the crisis said on Wednesday he faced a formidable task but was confident he could get all sides to sit down and talk.
"It's an extraordinarily difficult mission," Raymond Chretien, Canada's ambassador to Washington, told reporters.
Rwanda confirmed on Wednesday some of its troops entered Zaire "after they hit our territory and killed our people."
The Kinshasa government accuses Rwanda and Burundi, whose armies and governments are dominated by Tutsis, of backing the Banyamulenge Tutsis in South Kivu against the Zairean army.
